The splitEight servers · four datacenters

Our metal. Every machine behind its own walls.

Each cube is a machine: its own budget, its own Postgres and domain. A noisy neighbour cannot reach you, and you cannot reach it.

What you see is our own metal carrying many machines, each behind its own walls. That is the whole product.

Client machinesAgent machinesFree capacity
What you getOne namespace · one bill

A machine is a computer that is only yours.

A machine is one dedicated Kubernetes namespace — kdeploy-<project>-<group> — with its own resources, its own addons, its own domains, its own team and one bill. Everything you run lives inside it as a pod. The Kubernetes part is run by us and invisible to you: you see a box with a slider.

Isolated by defaultBare-metal speed behind ironclad kernel and network walls — no leaky multi-tenant hosts.
  • Hardened network perimeter — every machine sealed in its own namespace, ingress and egress policy enforced. Neighbours cannot sniff your traffic or reach your pods.
  • Kernel sandboxing — heavy workloads and AI agents run inside gVisor sandboxes, fully isolated from the host kernel.
  • Envelope-vault secrets — keys and env vars under AES-256-GCM envelope encryption with tamper-evident audit logs. Protected secrets never return plaintext.
Everything insideKill five SaaS subscriptions — the whole production stack lives in one machine.
  • Auto-healing data — two-instance PostgreSQL clusters with streaming failover, three-node NATS JetStream RAFT.
  • Storage, cron and edge TLS — Redis, MongoDB, S3 object storage, CronJobs and custom domains with automated TLS. No external addons.
  • Full-stack telemetry — Grafana dashboards for metrics, logs and traces, plus Sentry-compatible error tracking, all in one CLI.
One billOne budget, unlimited pods — no per-pod tax.
  • Unified resource wallet — a machine is a fixed budget of vCPU, RAM and storage on one predictable subscription.
  • Pods without bills — every extra web, worker or release pod shares the machine's budget. No new fees.
  • Stage and prod groups — sibling machines with isolated networks, each its own namespace and database, on the same budget.
Workloads and previewsZero-downtime rollouts and an instant preview for every pull request.
  • Targeted pods — run workloads as web, worker or release, each owning its repo, branch, domain and ports.
  • Zero-downtime rollouts — rolling or recreate strategies with 5xx watchers and instant auto-rollback.
  • PR preview URLs — every pull request spins up an isolated preview with its own namespace and URL.

A pod is one workload inside a machine: web, worker or release. Each pod has its own repo, branch, port, replicas and rollout. PR previews get their own namespace and URL.

AddonsManaged or dedicated

The stack, one toggle each.

Managed on shared instances, or dedicated inside your machine with its own volume and size. Attach to any pod in one command.

Postgres

Managed or dedicated. pgvector and Timescale on request. Scheduled backups to a private bucket.

Redis

Managed with a key prefix, or dedicated with AOF and search modules.

S3 storage

Your own bucket and IAM user on SeaweedFS, with a CDN URL.

NATS

JetStream on its own volume, WebSocket in.

MongoDB

Per machine database, or dedicated.

SQL Server

For the pods that need it.

Meilisearch

Search with its own persistent volume.

Cron

Scheduled jobs from your pod image, with run history.

OAuth2 proxy

GitHub or Google login in front of any pod, no code.

Grafana

Dedicated per machine, wired read only to your own telemetry.

GlitchTip

Sentry compatible error tracking, one DSN per environment.

AI

An OpenAI compatible endpoint in the cluster: a current open model for chat, one for embeddings, metered per machine.

Built for agentsCLI · --json · MCP

Your agent already knows how to use it.

The CLI is the product. One binary, every command with --json, clear errors an agent can act on. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or a shell script: they all deploy the same way. There is an MCP server if you prefer tool calls.

Deploy from the chatusectl machines create, usectl deploy, usectl logs --follow. No plugin needed.
Agents that live hereAdd a resident agent — Hermes, the open source AI agent, or OpenClaw, the open source browser agent — and it runs around the clock with its own memory, its own headless browser and a local model. One agent, one machine, its own walls.
Read what happenedLogs, metrics, traces and pod insights through the same CLI, so the agent that deployed can also debug.
~/radio-bot · usectl-cli v2.0.4 
$ usectl machines create radio-bot --repo github.com/you/radio-bot --postgres$ usectl addons add radio-bot --type hermes✓ hermes agent pod running. telegram gateway connected.$ usectl logs radio-bot --follow

FAQPlain answers

Questions people ask

Is a machine a VM?
No. A machine is a dedicated Kubernetes namespace — kdeploy-<project>-<group> — with a network policy, a quota and its own secrets on nodes we operate. The pods you run live inside it. Container isolation, not a microVM. We say that plainly because it matters for some workloads.
Can I leave?
Yes. Your Dockerfile, your Postgres dump and your bucket run anywhere. If we disappeared tomorrow your stack still works.
Where is my data?
On bare metal we own at Hetzner in Falkenstein, Germany. With self hosted usectl, on your own hardware.
What about backups?
Managed Postgres is dumped nightly at the platform level. Dedicated Postgres gets scheduled backups to a private bucket only that database can reach.
Is there a bandwidth meter or a seat fee?
No and no. The sticker is the ceiling. The honest fine print: a single request tops out at 100 MB, and machines cannot talk to each other.
Do I need Docker?
Not for Next.js, Vite, Node or static sites. For anything else, a Dockerfile.
Who is behind this?
systemctl, a team in Tbilisi, Georgia. We own and run our servers at Hetzner ourselves.
What happens to my data if you shut down?
Your Dockerfile, your Postgres dump and your bucket already run anywhere. Backups are yours to download any time — from the Postgres panel, or straight over the S3 API.
